goals: Compare procedure-oriented and object-oriented programming with an example
State the limitations of the first and the advantages of the second
Define data abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism with original examples

slides.heading: Two ways to build a program
slides.body_md: Part 1: **procedure-oriented** and **object-oriented** programming, and the four **principles** of object-oriented programming.

nodes.label: Two ways to organise a program

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: two ways to organise a program, procedure-oriented, object-oriented, the four principles, abstraction and encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to this revision of how programs are organised. First we compare two approaches: building a program from procedures, and building it from objects. Then we study the four principles of object-oriented programming: data abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. By the end you will be able to explain each one with an example of your own.

slides.heading: Procedure-oriented programming
slides.body_md: A **procedure-oriented** program is a list of procedures (functions) that work on data. The main task is split into smaller procedures.

rows: Often shared; moves freely between functions
Top-down: split the main task into smaller procedures
Shared data is unprotected: any function can change it by mistake
A change in the data may force changes in many functions
Real-world things are hard to model as separate procedures

visual.alt: Table of procedure-oriented programming: the procedure is the main unit, data is shared and moves freely, design is top-down, and three limitations: unprotected shared data, changes spreading to many functions, and poor modelling of real-world things

slides.narration: In procedure oriented programming the program is a collection of procedures, also called functions. The main task is broken into smaller tasks, and each becomes a function. This is the top down approach. The data is usually shared by the functions, so it moves freely between them, and that freedom is the source of its limitations, which you can see in the table.

visual.caption: Procedure-oriented versus object-oriented organisation.

slides.narration: Look at the picture. On the left, three functions all reach into one shared pile of data, so any of them can change it. On the right, each object keeps its own data hidden inside and offers methods. When one object needs something from another, it sends a message by calling a method. Data is protected, because it can be changed only through the methods of its own object.

slides.heading: Object-oriented programming
slides.body_md: An **object-oriented** program is built from **objects**, each combining data and the methods that work on it. The data is hidden.

rows: The object: data and methods together
Hidden inside the object; reached through its methods
Bottom-up: design the objects, then combine them
Data hiding protects data from accidental change
Inheritance reuses classes, so less new code is written
Programs are easier to maintain and model the real world

visual.alt: Table of object-oriented programming: the object is the main unit, data is hidden, design is bottom-up, and three advantages: data hiding, reuse through inheritance, and easier maintenance and modelling

slides.narration: In object oriented programming the program is built from objects. An object combines data with the methods that work on that data. The data is hidden from the outside, and the design is bottom up: we design the small parts first and combine them. The advantages are data hiding, reuse through inheritance, and programs that are easier to maintain and closer to the real world.

slides.heading: Quick check: which approach?
slides.body_md: Read the description and choose.
slides.narration: Look for the clue in the description. Are the data and the actions bundled together, or are functions working on shared data?

slides.heading: Comparing the two approaches

rows: On the data and the objects
Shared and open to all functions

visual.alt: Comparison table of procedure-oriented and object-oriented programming on six bases: what the program is built from, emphasis, data, approach, reuse and security of data

slides.narration: Here is the full comparison. A procedure oriented program is built from procedures and puts the emphasis on the steps. An object oriented program is built from objects and puts the emphasis on data. Procedure oriented data is shared and open, object oriented data is hidden. One is top down, the other bottom up, and only the second reuses classes through inheritance.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a school canteen in two styles
slides.body_md:
An imagined school canteen sells snacks. See how the same job looks in each style.

1. **Procedure-oriented:** shared arrays hold the names and stock; functions edit them.
2. **Object-oriented:** a class Snack holds the name and stock and has its own methods.
3. Adding a new feature touches many functions in the first design, but only one class in the second.

rows: Arrays names and stock shared by all functions
A class Snack with the data members name and stock
Function sell(i, n) edits stock[i] directly
The object runs its own method sell(n)
Every function that touches the arrays may change
Extend the arrays and check every function
Create one more object with new

visual.alt: Table comparing a school canteen program written two ways: shared arrays and functions versus a Snack class with its own methods, across keeping stock, selling, adding a price field and adding a new snack

slides.narration: Imagine a school canteen program. In the procedure oriented design, two shared arrays hold the names and the stock, and every function edits them directly. In the object oriented design, a class called Snack holds the name and stock, and each snack object sells itself with its own method. When a price field is added, the first design may change many functions; the second changes only the class.

slides.heading: Which approach fits?

rows: A ten-line program to add two numbers
Small, one task, no entities to model
A library system with members, books and cards
Real entities with their own data and actions
Data that must not be changed by accident
A big program that will grow for years
Classes can be reused and extended

visual.alt: Table of four situations with the better approach and the reason: a tiny program suits the procedure-oriented style; a library system, protected data and a growing program suit the object-oriented style

slides.narration: Neither approach is wrong in every case. A tiny program that adds two numbers has no real entities, so a few procedures are enough. A library system has members, books and cards, each with its own data and actions, so objects fit naturally. When data must be protected, or when a large program will keep growing, the object oriented approach is the better choice.

visual.caption: The four principles of object-oriented programming.

slides.narration: Object oriented programming rests on four principles. Data abstraction shows only the essential features and hides the details. Encapsulation binds data and methods into one unit, the class, and restricts access. Inheritance lets one class acquire the properties of another. Polymorphism means one name with many forms. The next slides take them one at a time.

slides.heading: Data abstraction and encapsulation
slides.body_md: Abstraction answers **what is shown**; encapsulation answers **how data and methods are packaged and protected**.

rows: Show only the essential features and hide the details
A metro gate opens when you tap a card; the balance check stays hidden
Bind data and methods into one unit, the class, and restrict access to the data
A medicine capsule keeps its contents sealed inside one shell

visual.alt: Table of two principles: data abstraction (show essentials, hide details; a metro gate that opens on a tap) and encapsulation (bind data and methods in a class and restrict access; a medicine capsule)

slides.narration: Data abstraction means showing only the essential features and hiding the details. When you tap a card at a metro gate, you see the gate open, not the balance check behind it. Encapsulation means binding data and methods into one unit, the class, and restricting access to the data from outside. A medicine capsule is a good picture: everything sits sealed inside one shell.

slides.narration: Ask yourself for each situation: is something being hidden, packaged, reused or given many forms?

slides.heading: Inheritance
slides.body_md:
**Inheritance** is the process by which a class acquires the properties (data members and methods) of another class.

The class that gives is the **superclass**; the class that receives is the **subclass**.

nodes.label: Subclass ElectricBike: all of Bike, plus battery and charge()

visual.alt: Flow showing that the subclass ElectricBike acquires everything in the superclass Bike (wheels, pedal and brake) and adds a battery and a charge method
visual.caption: Inheritance: a subclass acquires the properties of its superclass.

slides.narration: Inheritance lets a class acquire the properties of another class. The class that gives its properties is the superclass, also called the base or parent class. The class that receives them is the subclass, also called the derived or child class. An electric bike class can inherit everything from a bike class and add only a battery and a charge method. That is reuse without rewriting.

slides.heading: Polymorphism
slides.body_md:
**Polymorphism** means one name, many forms. In Java, **method overloading** is the example: several methods share a name but differ in their parameter lists.

```java
void greet()
void greet(String name)
void greet(String name, int times)
```

visual.alt: Table of three calls of the overloaded method greet: with no argument it prints Hello, with a name it prints Hello and the name, and with a name and a count it prints the name that many times
visual.caption: One method name, three forms, chosen by the arguments.

slides.narration: Polymorphism means one name with many forms. In Java, the example you need is method overloading: one class has several methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the version that matches the arguments in the call. The table shows a method called show used with one number, with a word, and with two numbers.

slides.narration: The teacher uses one name for several forms. Which principle has exactly that meaning?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: name the principle
slides.body_md:
Read each situation and name the principle.

1. Look for hiding details, then for binding and protecting, then for acquiring, and finally for one name with many forms.
2. Give a reason in one short sentence.

rows: A phone user taps the camera icon and a photo is saved; the steps inside are hidden
A class Account keeps balance private and offers deposit() and withdraw()
Class Laptop acquires everything in class Computer and adds a battery
A method area() is written for a circle and again for a rectangle

visual.alt: Table pairing four situations with principles: a phone camera icon with data abstraction, a class with private balance with encapsulation, Laptop acquiring Computer with inheritance, and area for circle and rectangle with polymorphism

slides.narration: Let us practise naming principles. The phone camera icon saves a photo while the steps stay hidden, so that is data abstraction. A class that keeps its balance private and offers deposit and withdraw methods shows encapsulation. A laptop class that acquires everything in a computer class shows inheritance. An area method written for both a circle and a rectangle shows polymorphism.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Objects with data and methods, hidden data, bottom-up
Data and methods bound in a class, access restricted
A subclass acquires the properties of a superclass
One name, many forms; for example method overloading

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: procedure-oriented, object-oriented, data abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A procedure oriented program is a set of functions on shared data, designed top down. An object oriented program is a set of objects with hidden data, designed bottom up. Data abstraction shows the essentials, encapsulation binds and protects, inheritance reuses a parent class, and polymorphism gives one name many forms.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **two** points for limitations or advantages when the question carries two marks.
Use a table or two clear columns when asked to **compare** or **distinguish**.
Always add a small, original example to a definition of a principle.
Do not mix up abstraction (what is shown) and encapsulation (how it is packaged).
Procedure-oriented is top-down; object-oriented is bottom-up.
slides.narration: A few exam tips. When a question asks for two limitations or two advantages, write two clear points. For a comparison, use a table with the same bases on both sides. Add a short example of your own to each definition. Take care not to mix up abstraction, which is about what is shown, with encapsulation, which is about packaging and protecting. And remember: procedure oriented is top down, object oriented is bottom up.

Then we list the features of Java and finish with the heart of the chapter: objects, classes, creating objects with new, and message passing between objects.

slides.heading: Applets and applications
slides.body_md:
An **applet** was a Java program that ran inside a web browser. An **application** is a stand-alone program with a **main** method.

*Dated note:* the applet API was deprecated in Java 9 and marked for removal in Java 17, so applets no longer run in modern browsers (as of 2024). The syllabus still names them.

Methods called by the browser or applet viewer

slides.narration: Java programs come in two kinds. An applet was a program written to run inside a web browser. An application is a stand alone program that starts from its main method. Applets are now obsolete: the applet interface was deprecated in Java nine and marked for removal in Java seventeen, and modern browsers no longer run them. The syllabus still names them, so know the definition.

sections.heading: 1. Procedure-oriented programming
sections.body_md:
In **procedure-oriented programming** a program is a list of **procedures** (functions) that work on data. The main task is split into smaller tasks, each written as a function (**top-down** design). The data is usually shared, and moves freely from function to function.

**Limitations**
- Shared data is unprotected: any function can change it by mistake.
- A change in the data may force changes in many functions.
- Real-world things are hard to model as separate procedures.

key_terms.definition_md: A programming approach in which the program is a set of procedures (functions) that act on shared data, designed top-down.

sections.heading: 2. Object-oriented programming and the comparison
sections.body_md:
In **object-oriented programming** (OOP) a program is built from **objects**. Each object combines **data** and the **methods** that work on it, and the data is **hidden** from outside. Design is **bottom-up**.

**Advantages**
- Data hiding protects data from accidental change.
- Inheritance lets classes be reused and extended.
- Programs are easier to maintain and model the real world.

Imagined example: a school canteen as shared arrays and functions (procedure-oriented) or as a class `Snack` with its own `sell()` method (object-oriented).

sections.heading: 3. Principles of OOP
sections.body_md:
- **Data abstraction:** showing only the essential features and hiding the details.
- **Encapsulation:** binding data and methods into one unit, the class, and restricting access to the data.
- **Inheritance:** a class acquires the properties (data members and methods) of another class; the giver is the **superclass**, the receiver the **subclass**.
- **Polymorphism:** one name, many forms; method overloading gives several methods with one name and different parameter lists.

```java
void perimeter(int side)
void perimeter(int length, int breadth)
```

The call `perimeter(5)` and the call `perimeter(5, 3)` run different methods.

The ability of one name, such as a method name, to have many forms.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up abstraction (what is shown) and encapsulation (how data and methods are packaged and protected).
- Saying procedure-oriented is bottom-up; it is top-down.
- Writing that bytecode is machine code; it is the intermediate code that the JVM executes.
- Forgetting `new`: declaring `Fan f;` does not create an object.
- Thinking two objects share their data members; each has its own copy.
- Treating a copied reference as a copied object.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definitions and distinctions (2 marks): one point per mark, each with a short example.
- Output questions (2 marks): the exact output, line by line.
- Programs (15 marks): class and method structure, input, correct logic, output format, and variable description or comments.

questions.stem_md: In procedure-oriented programming a program is mainly organised as:

options.text_md: a set of objects that hide their own data
a set of procedures (functions) that work on data
a hierarchy of classes only
a set of web pages that run in a browser

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a set of procedures (functions) that work on data. A procedure-oriented program is a list of procedures or functions called in order. Objects that hide their data belong to the object-oriented approach, a class hierarchy is only one tool of that approach, and browser pages have nothing to do with how code is organised.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a limitation of procedure-oriented programming?

options.text_md: The program cannot be divided into functions
Loops and decisions cannot be used
The program can run only on one make of computer
Data is open to every function, so a wrong change made in one function can damage the whole program

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Data is open to every function, so a wrong change made in one function can damage the whole program. In a procedure-oriented program data is usually shared and not protected. Functions are exactly what the approach uses, and it has loops and decisions like any other style. It is also not tied to one make of computer.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an advantage of object-oriented programming?

options.text_md: Data is kept inside objects, so it is safer from accidental change
Every function can change every data item directly
The whole program is written as one long list of steps
Objects are not allowed to have methods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Data is kept inside objects, so it is safer from accidental change. Hiding data inside objects protects it from outside changes. Free access by every function and one long list of steps describe the procedure-oriented style, and an object without methods would have no behaviour.

questions.stem_md: The object-oriented approach to designing a program is:

options.text_md: top-down: the main task is split into smaller and smaller functions
sideways: the classes are written only after the program is finished
bottom-up: objects are designed first and combined to make the program
neither: the object-oriented approach has no design method

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** bottom-up: objects are designed first and combined to make the program. Object-oriented design starts from the objects (the small parts) and builds upwards. The top-down splitting of the main task is the procedure-oriented approach.

questions.stem_md: For the imagined shop Lakshmi Stores a programmer writes the functions addStock(), sell() and report(). All three read and change the same global arrays of item names and quantities. Which approach has been used?

options.text_md: Object-oriented programming
Inheritance-based programming
Procedure-oriented programming
Applet programming

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Procedure-oriented programming. The program is a set of functions that share global data, which is the procedure-oriented approach. An object-oriented design would put the item data and its methods together in a class such as Item or Stock.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Object-oriented programming follows a top-down approach, while procedure-oriented programming follows a bottom-up approach.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The two are the wrong way round: procedure-oriented programming is top-down and object-oriented programming is bottom-up.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a procedure-oriented program the data is more exposed to accidental change than in an object-oriented program.

**Reason (R):** In a procedure-oriented program the data is usually shared by many functions, while in an object-oriented program an object keeps its data and changes it through its own methods.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both statements are true and R explains A: because many functions can reach the shared data, any of them can change it by mistake, whereas an object guards its data behind its methods.

questions.stem_md: State two limitations of procedure-oriented programming.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: unprotected shared data; changes ripple through many functions; poor modelling of real-world entities.

answer.model_answer_md: Data is shared by many functions and is not protected, so a function can change it by mistake. Because of this, a change in the data or in one function may force changes in many other functions, and real-world things are hard to model as separate procedures.

questions.stem_md: State two advantages of object-oriented programming over procedure-oriented programming.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: data hiding; reuse through inheritance; easier maintenance; closer to real-world modelling.

answer.model_answer_md: Data is hidden inside objects, so it is protected from accidental change. A class can be reused and extended through inheritance, so new programs need less new code, and the program is easier to maintain because it is built from independent objects.

questions.stem_md: Binding data and the methods that use it into a single unit called a class, and restricting access to that data from outside, is called:

options.text_md: encapsulation
inheritance
polymorphism
compilation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** encapsulation. This is the definition of encapsulation. Inheritance is one class acquiring the properties of another, polymorphism is one name with many forms, and compilation is the translation of source code.

questions.stem_md: A passenger taps a travel card on a gate and the gate opens. The passenger does not know how the reader checks the balance. Which OOP principle does this best illustrate?

options.text_md: Inheritance
Polymorphism
Garbage collection
Data abstraction

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Data abstraction. The passenger sees only the essential feature (tap and enter) while the working of the reader stays hidden, which is data abstraction. Nothing here is a class acquiring features, one name doing several jobs, or memory being freed.

questions.stem_md: The imagined class ElectricBike takes over all the data members and methods of the class Bike and adds a battery level. Which OOP principle is used?

options.text_md: Data abstraction
Inheritance
Method overloading
Message passing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Inheritance. ElectricBike acquires the properties of Bike, so Bike is the superclass and ElectricBike the subclass: this is inheritance. Overloading needs several methods with one name, and abstraction is about hiding details.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an example of polymorphism in Java?

options.text_md: Several methods of one class that share a name but have different parameter lists
Keeping the data members of a class private
A class acquiring the methods of another class
Compiling a source file to a class file

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Several methods of one class that share a name but have different parameter lists. Polymorphism means one name with many forms, and method overloading is the example in this syllabus. Private data members show encapsulation, acquiring the methods of another class is inheritance, and compiling has nothing to do with the principles.

options.text_md: `number 4 / number four / sum 9`
`number 4 / text four / sum 9`
`number 4 / text four / number 5`
`text 4 / text four / sum 9`

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** `number 4 / text four / sum 9`. The call with one int picks show(int), the call with a String picks show(String), and the call with two ints picks show(int, int), which prints their sum, 9. The compiler decides by the number and types of the arguments.

questions.stem_md: A teacher says: "The same name area() can be used to find the area of a circle from one value and of a rectangle from two values." Which OOP principle is she describing?

options.text_md: Encapsulation
Inheritance
Polymorphism
Data hiding only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Polymorphism. One method name serving several forms, chosen by the arguments, is polymorphism (method overloading). Encapsulation is binding data and methods in a class, and inheritance is acquiring the properties of another class.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is NOT a principle of object-oriented programming?

options.text_md: Inheritance
Encapsulation
Polymorphism
Iteration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Iteration. Iteration (repeating statements with a loop) is a programming construct, not an OOP principle. Data abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism are the principles.

questions.stem_md: A class keeps its data members private and gives public methods to read and change them. Which principle is mainly at work?

options.text_md: Inheritance, because the class acquires data from another class
Polymorphism, because the methods have different names
Message passing, because no object calls any method
Encapsulation, because data and methods are bound in one class with controlled access

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Encapsulation, because data and methods are bound in one class with controlled access. Private data reached only through the class's own methods is encapsulation. No other class supplies data here (not inheritance), the methods are not one name in many forms, and outside code reaches the data by calling methods, which is message passing rather than its absence.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Data abstraction and encapsulation mean exactly the same thing.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** They are related but different: abstraction shows only the essential features and hides the details, while encapsulation binds data and methods into one class and restricts access to the data.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Encapsulation and data abstraction are two names for the same idea.

**Reason (R):** Encapsulation binds data and methods into one class and restricts access, while data abstraction presents only the essential features and hides the details.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false because the two ideas differ. R is true: it states the separate meaning of each principle.

questions.stem_md: In inheritance, the class that acquires the properties is the ___ class and the class that gives them is the ___ class.
questions.solution_md: The subclass (derived or child class) inherits from the superclass (base or parent class).

questions.stem_md: Match each situation in an imagined bicycle-repair shop with the OOP principle it shows.

options.text_md: A customer asks for a repair and sees only the receipt, not the repair steps
The tool kit and the instructions for using it are kept in one locked box
The new tandem bike model reuses the frame design of the standard model
One word, service, means one job for a bicycle and a different job for a rickshaw

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Seeing only the result is abstraction; binding the tools and instructions together with limited access is encapsulation; reusing a design is inheritance; one name with different forms is polymorphism.

questions.stem_md: Define encapsulation and give one original example from daily life.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the definition, one for a correct example.

answer.model_answer_md: Encapsulation is the binding of data and the methods that work on it into one unit, the class, and restricting access to the data from outside. Example: a medicine capsule keeps its ingredients sealed inside one shell.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: data and methods bound in a class, access restricted

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between data abstraction and encapsulation.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each principle stated correctly with its difference.

answer.model_answer_md: Data abstraction shows only the essential features of an object to the user and hides the working details. Encapsulation binds the data and the methods into one class and restricts access to the data. Abstraction is about what is shown; encapsulation is about how it is packaged and protected.
